evidence.excerpt: A module is identified by a module path , which is declared in a go.mod file , together with information about the module's dependencies.

For each required module version, the go command loads the go.mod file for that version and incorporates the requirements from that file. Once all requirements have been loaded, the go command resolves them using minimal version selection (MVS) to produce the build list .

The go.sum file contains cryptographic hashes of the module's direct and indirect dependencies. ... Each line in go.sum has three fields separated by spaces: a module path, a version (possibly ending with /go.mod ), and a hash.
A require directive declares a minimum required version of a given module dependency.  ...  An exclude directive prevents a module version from being loaded by the go command.
-mod=vendor tells the go command to use the vendor directory. In this mode, the go command will not use the network or the module cache.

After downloading a .mod or .zip file, the go command computes a cryptographic hash and checks that it matches a hash in the main module's go.sum file. ... If the computed hash does not match, the go command reports a security error and does not install the file in the module cache.

evidence.excerpt: The Swift Package Manager lets you share your code as a package, depend on and use other shared packages, as well as build, test, document, and run your code.

The package manager automatically resolves packages when you invoke [build or run]. ... When this file is present and you are resolving dependencies for the top-level (leaf) package of a dependency tree, the package manager uses the Package.resolved file as a cache of versions of the dependencies. ... Most SwiftPM commands implicitly invoke dependency resolution before running, and cancel with an error if dependencies cannot be resolved.

The package manager records the result of dependency resolution in a file named Package.resolved at the top-level of the package. ... you can keep a Package.resolved file in source control, or resolve it locally and pass it to a container image build process, in order to ensure another build uses the same versions of dependencies.

Use the version requirement when you declare the dependency to limit what the package manager can choose. The version requirement can be a range of possible semantic versions, a specific semantic version, a branch name, or a commit hash.

evidence.detail: M5 - built-in help text shipped by the toolchain under test: `swift package --help` (E2 explicitly admits shipped --help text), plus .../addingdependencies for the vendored-copy route
evidence.excerpt: --enable-dependency-cache/--disable-dependency-cache  Use a shared cache when fetching dependencies. (default: --enable-dependency-cache)   --skip-update  Skip updating dependencies from their remote during a resolution.   [addingdependencies] To use a local package as a dependency, use either [.package(path:)] to define it with the local path to the package.

The package manager records fingerprints of downloaded package versions so that it can perform [trust on first use] (TOFU). ... Package Version Origin / Fingerprint: Git repository = Git hash of the revision; Package registry = Checksum of the source archive. ... [--help] --enable-signature-validation/--disable-signature-validation  Validate signature of a signed package release downloaded from registry. (default: --enable-signature-validation)

Swift.reasoning: M = 6 and INSTALLED is true (S5, `swift package --version` executed here), so 100 and not 80. Two notes for an auditor. First, the manager selected is SwiftPM and not CocoaPods, even though Library Availability selected CocoaPods as Swift's index; the manager_selection_rule's first clause (ships with the official toolchain distribution) fires before the index clause and is not discretionary. Second, M3's pin for a source-control dependency is a git revision rather than a semantic version. That is the same latitude applied to Quidra's content hash under this metric, and denying it to one while granting it to the other would be exactly the asymmetry spec section 7 and the fairness_declaration forbid.

Zig.selected_manager: the Zig toolchain's built-in package manager (`zig fetch`, `zig build --fetch`, build.zig.zon), host: zig 0.16.0
Zig.manager_selection_reason: manager_selection_rule clause 1: package management ships with the official Zig toolchain distribution as subcommands and flags of the `zig` binary itself. The index fallback clause is not reached, and could not have been used in any case, because Library Availability recorded no qualifying index for Zig.
Zig.availability_state: S5 (present on this host and executed)
criteria_failed: M3 - NOT SATISFIED. Zig produces no lockfile and no equivalent single artifact enumerating the resolved closure. build.zig.zon lists only the package's DIRECT dependencies, each as a url+hash or a path; the hashes of transitive dependencies live in each dependency's own build.zig.zon, so no artifact the manager writes records the exact resolved identity of every direct AND transitive dependency. `zig fetch --save` writes only into the direct-dependency table. No 'lock' string appears in `zig build --help`, `zig fetch --help`, the generated build.zig.zon template, or the official build-system documentation.

M4 - NOT SATISFIED. The manifest expresses no version constraint or range on a dependency at all. The toolchain-generated build.zig.zon states that each dependency must provide a url+hash or a path; the only version-shaped fields are the package's own `.version` and `.minimum_zig_version` (a constraint on the Zig compiler, not on a dependency). The manifest's own comment states that the hash, not the url and not a version, is the source of truth.

Zig.reasoning: M = 4, which is the 60 / Substantial criterion. Not 80, because 80 needs M >= 5 and Zig fails both M3 and M4: its design deliberately replaces version resolution with content addressing, so there is neither a version constraint to write nor a resolved-version closure to record. Not 40, because four indicators are positively evidenced, two of them from the toolchain's own shipped text. Zig's genuine strengths under this metric - recursive fetching of the whole dependency tree, an explicit documented statement that builds work without connectivity once fetched, and mandatory hash verification that refuses a mismatched package - are all scored normally.

cross_language_consistency_note: The six indicators are binary and documentary, so the level is mechanical once each indicator is decided; the only place where the same words could have meant different things across languages is M3 and M4, and both were pinned to a single discriminator applied in the frozen collection order. M3 discriminator, fixed while scoring C++ and Java (the third and fifth languages collected) and applied unchanged thereafter: does the manager emit ONE artifact that enumerates the entire direct-plus-transitive closure with a pin that fixes exactly which artifact is used, as stated in first-party documentation? Manifest-side pinning that merely DETERMINES the closure does not qualify. Under it: Rust (Cargo.lock), Go (go.sum - path, version and hash for direct and indirect dependencies), npm (package-lock.json - the exact tree), Python (pylock.toml and pip freeze), Swift (Package.resolved) and Quidra (quidra.lock) pass; vcpkg (registry baseline plus overrides, inside the manifest), Maven for both Java and Kotlin (no lock artifact at all), and Zig (direct dependencies only, hashes of transitive ones living in other manifests) fail. The pin itself is allowed to be a version, a git revision or a content hash - Swift records a git revision for source-control dependencies and Quidra records a SHA-256 - because refusing a content hash for one language while accepting a revision hash for another is exactly the asymmetry the fairness rule forbids; this latitude was settled on Swift, which was collected eighth, before Quidra. M4 discriminator: the manifest must be able to express something other than one exact version for a dependency, with the syntax documented. Maven ranges, npm and Cargo semver operators, vcpkg 'version>=', SwiftPM version ranges and Go's documented minimum-version 'require' plus 'exclude' all pass; Zig (url+hash or path only) and Quidra (no manifest and no version concept) fail. INSTALLED was decided uniformly from the tool_availability_states table by running each manager's documented version command on this host: pip, cargo, go, npm, swift package, zig and quidra are S5; vcpkg, mvn and gradle are absent and therefore S3, which by the table's own wording does not rescue INSTALLED. Every language was examined under exactly the two evidence sources the rubric names for this metric, E1 and E2, with no language scored from an E-source another was not; no language was scored from reputation or from general knowledge. As a check on the final assignments: the three languages at 80 (C++, Java, Kotlin) all fail M3 and only M3; the two at 60 (Zig, Quidra) each fail exactly two indicators; the five at 100 satisfy all six and had their manager executed here. No two languages with the same satisfied-indicator set received different levels, and no two with different sets received the same level by accident - Java and Kotlin share a level because the frozen rule routes them to the same manager, and Zig and Quidra share a level from different failures (Zig has a manifest with no constraints and no closure record; Quidra has a closure record but no manifest at all), which is a genuine tie and is reported as such under global_rules.tie_handling.
limitations: Accession dates. Every URL in this record was retrieved on 2026-09-19, two days after the frozen evidence_cutoff_date of 2026-09-17. The evidence_window rule requires only that the evidence EXISTED and was publicly retrievable on or before the cutoff, and permits collection to continue until Standard scoring completes; every statement relied on describes a long-standing documented capability of the manager, not a change published in that two-day window. No claim in this file rests on a page created after the cutoff. This applies identically to all ten languages.

Documentation version drift. pip's stable documentation renders as v26.2.1 while the host's pip is 26.1.1, and npm's docs render as v11.19.1 while the host's npm is 11.3.0. E2 explicitly admits 'the toolchain version under test or the nearest published version'. The relied-on statements (pip lock / pip freeze / hash-checking mode; package-lock.json, semver ranges, offline config, integrity) are present in both. No other language showed drift.

M3 for Quidra is the one indicator in this metric whose outcome turns on reading 'the exact resolved version' as admitting a content hash where the language has no version concept. quidra.lock demonstrably enumerates the full direct-plus-transitive closure and is demonstrably enforced (both verified by executed commands, including a tampering test), but it records SHA-256 values, not versions. An auditor reading 'version' strictly would fail M3, giving Quidra M = 3 and a score of 40 instead of 60. The same reading would also have to revisit Swift, whose Package.resolved records a git revision hash rather than a version for source-control dependencies.

M4 for Go is the second such indicator. Go has no range syntax; its 'require' directive declares a documented MINIMUM version that minimal version selection may raise, and 'exclude' removes versions. This was scored as a constraint, satisfying M4. An auditor requiring an explicit range syntax would fail M4, giving Go M = 5 and a score of 80 instead of 100.

vcpkg, Maven and Gradle are absent from this host and no_installation_of_extra_software forbids installing them, so no C++, Java or Kotlin indicator could be verified by execution; all five satisfied indicators for each of those three rest on E2 documentation alone, while the five languages scoring 100 additionally had their manager executed here. This asymmetry changes no level in this metric (C++, Java and Kotlin are capped at 80 by M3 independently of INSTALLED), but the S3 states for vcpkg, mvn and gradle belong in host_limited_indicators.json.

Manager selection was forced by the frozen manager_selection_rule and, for C++, Java and Kotlin, depends on the index that the separately frozen Library Availability rule selected. For Kotlin this means Maven rather than Gradle, the tool Kotlin's own documentation leads with. The level is unaffected (Gradle would reach M = 6 with INSTALLED still false, which is also 80), but the choice is recorded so an auditor can re-derive it.

Quidra's toolchain was built from source on this host by the benchmark team, so no Quidra indicator can fail for a repackaging reason, whereas C++, Java and Kotlin lost host verification to states S3. This disclosure is required by global_rules.tool_availability_states.required_publication.asymmetry_disclosed.

No third-party or community documentation was used for any language. Where a manager is not published by the language's official_project_set (vcpkg for C++, Maven for Java and Kotlin), M1's second clause - 'or by the manager's own maintainers' - was the admitting clause, and that is recorded in each of those three records.
